## 7. Numerical examples

### 7.1. Example 1: Model-free systemic risk

We first consider the systemic-risk specialization of the LQR McKean-Vlasov control problem studied in Section 5. This example admits an explicit Riccati characterization of the continuous-time optimal policy and therefore provides a benchmark to compare our algorithm.

#### 7.1.1. Problem setup

We work in dimension $d=m=1$ and impose the systemic-risk relation $\bar{A}=-A$ in (22). The controlled population dynamics are therefore

$$ ds_{t}=\bigl(A(s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t})+Ba_{t}\bigr)\,dt+\gamma\,dB_{t},\qquad\bar{\mu}_{t}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x\,\mu_{t}(dx),\qquad\mu_{t}=\Law(s_{t}). $$

The running reward is the quadratic reward introduced in (23), and the entropy-regularized averaged reward is defined by (3). The exact optimal policy is obtained from the Riccati system in Section 5. We use this explicit solution as a reference to illustrate the model-free actor-critic algorithm introduced in Section 6.

#### 7.1.2. Policy parametrization, value approximation and gradient direction

Following the explicit LQR structure, we use the Gaussian policy class

$$ \displaystyle\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\left(\omega_{1}(s-\bar{\mu})+\omega_{2}\bar{\mu},\,\frac{\lambda}{2}N^{-1}\right),\qquad\omega=(\omega_{1},\omega_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. $$

The critic is parametrized by the quadratic law-value ansatz

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\theta}(\mu)=\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\,\bar{\mu}^{2}+\theta_{3}\,\operatorname{Var}(\mu),\qquad\theta=(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. $$

In this finite-dimensional setting, the Lions derivative of the critic is $\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}_{\theta}(\mu)(s)=2\theta_{2}\bar{\mu}+2\theta_{3}(s-\bar{\mu}).$ As in the LQR-MF-PhiBE approximation considered in Section 5, we use the drift-only surrogate and set $\widehat{\Sigma}=0$ in the empirical advantage. Thus, for a data point $(s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta},a_{\eta},s^{\prime}_{\eta},r_{\eta})$ , with $\bar{\mu}_{\eta}=\int x\,\mu_{\eta}(dx)$ , the sample advantage used in the actor update is

$$ \displaystyle\widehat{q}_{\eta}=r_{\eta}-\lambda\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a_{\eta}\mid s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta})+\widehat{b}_{\eta}\left(2\theta_{2}\bar{\mu}_{\eta}+2\theta_{3}(s_{\eta}-\bar{\mu}_{\eta})\right)-\beta\left(\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}\bar{\mu}_{\eta}^{2}+\theta_{3}\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{\eta})\right), $$

with $\hat{b}$ defined in (38). Since the policy variance is fixed, the score function is

$$ \displaystyle\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega}}(a_{\eta}\mid s_{\eta},\mu_{\eta})=\frac{a_{\eta}-\omega_{1}(s_{\eta}-\bar{\mu}_{\eta})-\omega_{2}\bar{\mu}_{\eta}}{\lambda(2N)^{-1}}\begin{pmatrix}s_{\eta}-\bar{\mu}_{\eta}\\
\bar{\mu}_{\eta}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Hence the empirical policy-gradient direction used in the experiment is computed by substituting (48) and (49) into (44), with either discounted weights $w_{\eta}=e^{-\beta t_{\eta}}\Delta t$ or uniform weights $w_{\eta}=1/N_{D}$ .

#### 7.1.3. Implementation and numerical results

Since the policy parametrization in (46) and the value-function ansatz (47) depend on the law only through $\bar{\mu}_{\eta}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{\eta})$ , in this example we do not need a full empirical representation of $\mu_{\eta}$ . Hence, for a fixed policy $\pi_{\omega}$ , we assume that the available data set is

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\omega}=\left\{\bigl(s_{\ell}^{i},\bar{\mu}^{i},\operatorname{Var}(\mu^{i}),a_{\ell}^{i},r_{\ell}^{i},(s_{\ell}^{i})^{\prime}\bigr):i=1,\ldots,N_{\rm steps},\ \ell=1,\ldots,L\right\}. $$

Here $N_{\rm steps}$ is the number of observed one-step transitions along each trajectory, and $L$ is the number of independent trajectories, obtained from independent samples of the initial law. We have $s_{\ell}^{i}\sim\mu^{i}$ , $a_{\ell}^{i}\sim\pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s_{\ell}^{i},\mu^{i})$ , $r_{\ell}^{i}=r(s_{\ell}^{i},\mu^{i},a_{\ell}^{i})$ , and $(s_{\ell}^{i})^{\prime}$ denotes the state observed after one time step $\Delta t$ .

To reduce artificial sources of noise, the data are generated exactly from the LQR dynamics, thereby avoiding an additional numerical time-discretization error. More precisely, $(s_{\ell}^{i})^{\prime}$ is sampled from the explicit transition law (30), while the moments of the law are propagated through the closed equations associated with the current policy: $\dot{\bar{\mu}}_{t}=(A+\bar{A}+B\omega_{2})\bar{\mu}_{t}$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{t})=2(A+B\omega_{1})\operatorname{Var}(\mu_{t})+\gamma^{2}$ .

In the numerical experiment we use $N_{\rm steps}=50$ , $L=200$ , and $\Delta t=0.05$ . The numerical parameters are

$$ \displaystyle A=-1,\quad\bar{A}=1,\quad B=1,\quad Q=1,\quad\bar{Q}=1,\quad N=0.5,\quad\beta=1,\quad\gamma=0.5,\quad\lambda=0.2. $$

The initial law is $\mu=\mathcal{N}(1,1)$ . The empirical estimators entering (48), (49) and (44) are computed from $\mathcal{D}_{\omega}$ .

#### 7.1.4. Comparison with the time-discrete Bellman problem

The previous experiment evaluates the LQR-MF-PhiBE approximation of the continuous-time control problem. We now compare this construction with a different way of using observations at time step $\Delta t$ : instead of incorporating the one-step information into the continuous-time HJB structure, one may first discretize the controlled dynamics and then solve the resulting time-discrete Bellman problem.

Let $\rho_{\Delta t}(\cdot\mid s,\mu,a)$ denote the one-step transition kernel induced by (30). The corresponding discretized entropy-regularized objective is

$$ \mathcal{V}_{\Delta t}^{\pi}(\mu):=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta i\Delta t}\,\Delta t\,r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\mu_{i})\,\bigg|\,\mu_{0}=\mu\right], $$

where the controlled Markov chain is defined by

$$ s_{i+1}\sim\rho_{\Delta t}(\cdot\mid s_{i},\mu_{i},a_{i}),\qquad a_{i}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{i},\mu_{i}),\qquad\mu_{i}=\Law(s_{i}). $$

The discrete-time problem still admits an explicit Gaussian optimizer. Set $\delta:=e^{-\beta\Delta t}$ and $B_{\Delta t}:=\Delta t\,\hat{B}$ , where $\hat{B}$ is the action coefficient in the one-step drift estimator (32). Set

$$ A_{\Delta t}:=I+\Delta t\,\hat{A},\qquad\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}:=I+\Delta t(\hat{A}+\hat{\bar{A}}),\qquad B_{\Delta t}:=\Delta t\,\hat{B},\qquad\delta:=e^{-\beta\Delta t}. $$

Then, the optimal policy of the discretization problem is given by

$$ \pi_{\Delta t}^{*}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\left(\bar{\pi}_{\Delta t}^{*}(s,\mu),\Sigma_{\Delta t}^{*}\right),\qquad\Sigma_{\Delta t}^{*}=\frac{\lambda\Delta t}{2}\left(\Delta t\,N+\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\right)^{-1}, $$

with

$$ \displaystyle\bar{\pi}_{\Delta t}^{*}(s,\mu)= \displaystyle-\left[\left(\Delta t\,N+\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\right)^{-1}\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}A_{\Delta t}\right](s-\bar{\mu}) \displaystyle-\left[\left(\Delta t\,N+\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\right)^{-1}\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}\right]\bar{\mu}. $$

Here the matrices $K_{\Delta t}$ and $\Lambda_{\Delta t}$ are the stabilizing solutions of

$$ \displaystyle K_{\Delta t} \displaystyle=\Delta t\,Q+\delta A_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}A_{\Delta t}-\delta^{2}A_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\left(\Delta t\,N+\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\right)^{-1}B_{\Delta t}^{\top}K_{\Delta t}A_{\Delta t}, \displaystyle\Lambda_{\Delta t} \displaystyle=\Delta t\,(Q+\bar{Q})+\delta\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}-\delta^{2}\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\left(\Delta t\,N+\delta B_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}B_{\Delta t}\right)^{-1}B_{\Delta t}^{\top}\Lambda_{\Delta t}\widetilde{A}_{\Delta t}. $$

The optimal policy characterization is obtained by combining the time-discrete mean-field LQ framework of [18] with the entropy-regularized one-step Bellman minimization of [29]. The former motivates the discrete mean-field LQ structure, while the latter yields a Gaussian optimizer over randomized feedback policies, with covariance depending on $\Delta t$ .

For fixed $\Delta t>0$ , neither the discrete optimizer $\pi_{\Delta t}^{*}$ nor the LQR-MF-PhiBE optimizer $\hat{\pi}^{*}$ is expected to coincide exactly with the continuous-time optimizer $\pi^{*}$ . The question is therefore which of the two finite- $\Delta t$ approximations is closer to $\pi^{*}$ . To compare policies, for Gaussian feedback laws

$$ \pi_{i}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\left(-L_{c}^{i}(s-\bar{\mu})-L_{m}^{i}\bar{\mu},\Sigma_{i}\right),\qquad i=1,2, $$

we use

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{2}(\pi_{1},\pi_{2}):=\left(\|L_{c}^{1}-L_{c}^{2}\|^{2}+\|L_{m}^{1}-L_{m}^{2}\|^{2}+\|\Sigma_{1}^{1/2}-\Sigma_{2}^{1/2}\|_{F}^{2}\right)^{1/2}. $$

In particular, for every compact set $K\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , there exists $C_{K}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\sup_{(s,\bar{\mu})\in K}\mathcal{W}_{2}\bigl(\pi_{1}(\cdot\mid s,\mu),\pi_{2}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)\bigr)\leq C_{K}\mathcal{E}_{2}(\pi_{1},\pi_{2}). $$

### 7.2. Example 2: Crowd aversion transport

We next test the model-free MF-PhiBE actor-critic method on a nonlinear two-dimensional McKean-Vlasov control problem. The objective is to transport the population toward a prescribed target location while penalizing concentration in regions of high crowd density. This experiment is formulated directly at the level of the population law.

#### 7.2.1. Problem setup

The controlled population law $\mu_{t}$ is generated by

$$ ds_{t}=m_{\omega}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,dt+\sigma\,dW_{t},\qquad m_{\omega}(s,\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}a\,\pi_{\omega}(da\mid s,\mu), $$

where $s_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , $a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , and $\sigma>0$ is fixed. The running reward is

$$ r(s,\mu,a)=-\left(\frac{1}{2}\|a\|^{2}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\|s-s_{\rm tar}\|^{2}+\gamma(K_{\eta}*\mu)(s)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|s\|^{2}\right). $$

Here $s_{\rm tar}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ is the target, $\kappa>0$ controls target attraction, $\gamma>0$ controls crowd aversion, and $\rho\geq 0$ is a mild confinement parameter used for numerical stability. The crowd-density term is

$$ (K_{\eta}*\mu)(s)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|s-y\|^{2}}{2\eta^{2}}\right)\mu(dy), $$

where $\eta>0$ is the kernel bandwidth. We consider the entropy-regularized reward introduced in (3). The law-level objective is the discounted infinite-horizon value $\mathcal{V}^{\pi_{\omega}}$ in (2).

#### Remark 7.1 (Interpretation of the reward).

The four terms in the running cost correspond, respectively, to control effort, target attraction, crowd aversion, and mild confinement. Since the controlled equation is linear and the control acts directly as a velocity field, the learned policy is expected to transport the population toward $s_{\rm tar}$ while avoiding excessive concentration of mass, with the confinement term preventing particles from drifting too far from the target region.

#### 7.2.2. Policy and value approximation

Motivated by the crowd-density term in the reward, we use Gaussian kernel features of the population law. Let $c_{1},\ldots,c_{M_{\mu}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ be grid centers and let $h>0$ be a bandwidth. We define

$$ u_{j}(\mu)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|y-c_{j}\|^{2}}{2h^{2}}\right)\mu(dy),\qquad j=1,\ldots,M_{\mu}. $$

We use a Gaussian policy with fixed exploration covariance,

$$ \pi_{\omega}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\left(m_{\omega}(s,\mu),\sigma_{a}^{2}I_{2}\right),\qquad m_{\omega}(s,\mu)=Wf(s,\mu),\qquad\omega\equiv W\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times d_{f}}, $$

where the feature vector $f(s,\mu)$ is given by

$$ f(s,\mu)=\Bigl(1,\,s,\,s-s_{\rm tar},\,\|s-s_{\rm tar}\|^{2},\,u_{1}(\mu),\ldots,u_{M_{\mu}}(\mu)\Bigr)^{\top}. $$

Thus, in this two-dimensional example, the number of actor features is $d_{f}=6+M_{\mu}$ . For the critic, we use the cylindrical approximation

$$ \mathcal{V}_{\theta}(\mu)=\theta^{\top}\Phi(u(\mu)),\qquad u(\mu)=(u_{1}(\mu),\ldots,u_{M_{\mu}}(\mu)). $$

The feature map $\Phi$ contains the constant, the linear terms in $u$ , and all quadratic products:

$$ \Phi(u)=\Bigl(1,\,u_{1},\ldots,u_{M_{\mu}},\,\{u_{i}u_{j}\}_{1\leq i\leq j\leq M_{\mu}}\Bigr)^{\top}. $$

Thus, the critic has $1+M_{\mu}+M_{\mu}(M_{\mu}+1)/2$ features. The Lions derivatives $\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}_{\theta}(\mu)(x)$ and $D_{x}\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}_{\theta}(\mu)(x)$ are computed analytically from this cylindrical representation.

#### 7.2.3. Empirical MF-PhiBE critic and policy improvement

At policy iteration $k$ , we simulate $L$ independent empirical population trajectories, each consisting of $M$ particles and $N_{\rm steps}$ time steps. For trajectory $\ell$ and time index $i$ , the empirical law is

$$ \widehat{\mu}_{\ell}^{i}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta_{s_{\ell,j}^{i}}. $$

Given $\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}^{i}$ , we sample $a_{\ell,j}^{i}\sim\pi_{\omega_{k}}(\cdot\mid s_{\ell,j}^{i},\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}^{i}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,M,$ and generate the frozen-action transitions

$$ (s_{\ell,j}^{i})^{\prime}=s_{\ell,j}^{i}+a_{\ell,j}^{i}\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_{\ell,i,j},\qquad Z_{\ell,i,j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{2}). $$

Because the pointwise controlled drift in this example is $b(s,\mu,a)=a$ and the diffusion is constant, this frozen-action transition is exact and introduces no additional time-discretization error. The data available at policy iteration $k$ are

$$ \mathcal{D}_{\omega_{k}}=\left\{\bigl(s_{\ell,j}^{i},\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}^{i},a_{\ell,j}^{i},r_{\ell,j}^{i},(s_{\ell,j}^{i})^{\prime}\bigr):i=1,\ldots,N_{\rm steps},\ \ell=1,\ldots,L,\ j=1,\ldots,M\right\}. $$

The critic parameter $\theta$ is obtained from the Galerkin problem (42) using the one-step coefficient estimators $\widehat{b}_{\ell,i,j}$ and $\widehat{\Sigma}_{\ell,i,j}$ in (38). We use either discounted weights $w_{\ell,i}=e^{-\beta t_{i}}\Delta t/L$ or finite-horizon weights $w_{\ell,i}=\Delta t/L$ .

Once the MF-PhiBE critic has been computed, we evaluate the sample infinitesimal advantages $\widehat{q}_{\ell,i,j}$ in (45) and compute the empirical policy-gradient direction

$$ \widehat{\nabla J}(\omega_{k})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{i=0}^{N_{\rm steps}-1}w_{\ell,i}\,\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\left(\widehat{q}_{\ell,i,j}-\overline{q}_{\ell,i}\right)\nabla_{\omega}\log p_{\pi_{\omega_{k}}}\left(a_{\ell,j}^{i}\mid s_{\ell,j}^{i},\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}^{i}\right), $$

where $\overline{q}_{\ell,i}:=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\widehat{q}_{\ell,i,j},$ and with score term given by the explicit expression

$$ \nabla_{W}\log p_{\pi_{\omega_{k}}}(a\mid s,\mu)=\frac{1}{\sigma_{a}^{2}}\left(a-m_{\omega_{k}}(s,\mu)\right)f(s,\mu)^{\top}. $$

#### 7.2.4. Implementation and numerical results

For the numerical simulations, we use

$$ \sigma=0.2,\qquad\beta=0.1,\qquad\kappa=1000,\qquad\gamma=10,\qquad\eta=0.8,\qquad\rho=0.1,\qquad\lambda=2. $$

The initial law is concentrated near $x_{0}=(-2,0)^{\top}$ , with standard deviation $0.02$ , and the target is $x_{\rm tar}=(2,0)^{\top}$ . We train with $\Delta t=0.1$ , $T=4.5$ , $L=50$ empirical trajectories per policy update, $N_{\rm steps}=45$ time-steps, $M=40$ particles per empirical law, and $M_{\mu}=9$ law features, corresponding to a $3\times 3$ grid of centers $c_{1},\ldots,c_{9}$ . The policy uses fixed covariance $\sigma_{a}^{2}I_{2}$ , with $\sigma_{a}=0.25$ .

$$ (\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}-\beta)V^{\pi}(s,\mu)+\ell_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s,\mu)=0, $$

where $\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}$ being the generator on $\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ defined as

$$ \displaystyle(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}F)(s,\mu) \displaystyle:=b^{\pi}(s,\mu)\cdot\nabla_{s}F(s,\mu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma^{\pi}(s,\mu):\nabla^{2}_{ss}F(s,\mu) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Bigl[b^{\pi}(\xi,\mu)\cdot\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\Sigma^{\pi}(\xi,\mu):D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}F(s,\mu)(\xi)\Bigr]\,\mu(d\xi), $$

On the other hand, since the initial condition in (5) satisfies $s_{0}\sim\mu$ , conditioning on $s_{0}=s$ , using Fubini’s theorem, we have

$$ \displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\mu)&=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\ell_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,dt\,\bigg|\,\mu_{0}=\mu\right]=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\ell_{\lambda}^{\pi}(s_{t},\mu_{t})\,dt\,\bigg|\,s_{0}=s,\ \mu_{0}=\mu\right]\mu(ds)\\
&=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\,\mu(ds).\end{aligned} $$

Since $V^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2,2}_{\mathrm{poly}}$ , applying the Lions derivative formula for maps of the form $\mu\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)\,\mu(ds)$ [16, Section 5.6] yields

$$ \partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\mu)(x)=\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(x,\mu)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(x)\,\mu(ds), $$

and

$$ D_{x}\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\mu)(x)=\nabla^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(x,\mu)+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}D_{x}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(x)\,\mu(ds). $$

The polynomial bounds in the definition of $\mathcal{C}^{2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ follow directly from the corresponding bounds for $V^{\pi}$ . Hence $\mathcal{V}^{\pi}\in\mathcal{C}^{2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ . Using (56) and (57), we compute

$$ \displaystyle(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}\mathcal{V}^{\pi})(\mu) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[b^{\pi}(x,\mu)\cdot\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(x,\mu)+\frac{1}{2}\Sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu):\nabla^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(x,\mu)\right]\mu(dx) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left[b^{\pi}(x,\mu)\cdot\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(x)+\frac{1}{2}\Sigma^{\pi}(x,\mu):D_{x}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\mu)(x)\right]\mu(dx)\mu(ds) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}V^{\pi})(s,\mu)\,\mu(ds). $$

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}\mathcal{V}^{\pi})(\mu)-\beta\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\mu)+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\mu)=0. $$

Thus $\mathcal{V}^{\pi}$ solves (8).

We now prove uniqueness. Let $U\in\mathcal{C}^{2}_{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}))$ be another classical solution of (8). Applying the Itô-Lions formula to $e^{-\beta t}U(\mu_{t})$ gives

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-\beta t}U(\mu_{t})\right)=e^{-\beta t}\left[(\mathcal{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{\pi}U)(\mu_{t})-\beta U(\mu_{t})\right]=-e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\mu_{t}). $$

$$ U(\mu)=e^{-\beta T}U(\mu_{T})+\int_{0}^{T}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\mu_{t})\,dt. $$

$$ U(\mu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\mu_{t})\,dt=\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\mu). $$

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)|+|\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)(x)| \displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{\pi}}{\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi}}\bigl(1+|s|+|x|+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr), \displaystyle\|\nabla^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)\|+\|D_{x}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)(x)\| \displaystyle\leq\frac{C_{\pi}}{\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi}}\bigl(1+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr). $$

Combining these estimates with (56) gives

$$ \displaystyle|\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\nu)(x)| \displaystyle\leq|\nabla_{s}V^{\pi}(x,\nu)|+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)(x)|\,\nu(ds)\leq\frac{C_{\pi}}{\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi}}\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr). $$

$$ \displaystyle\|D_{x}\partial_{\mu}\mathcal{V}^{\pi}(\nu)(x)\| \displaystyle\leq\|\nabla^{2}_{ss}V^{\pi}(x,\nu)\|+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|D_{x}\partial_{\mu}V^{\pi}(s,\nu)(x)\|\,\nu(ds)\leq\frac{C_{\pi}}{\beta-\bar{\beta}_{\pi}}\bigl(1+|x|^{2}+m_{2}(\nu)\bigr). $$

This proves (9). ∎

$$ ds_{t}=b(s_{t},\mu_{t},a)\,dt+\sigma(s_{t},\mu_{t},a)\,dB_{t},\qquad s_{0}=s. $$

$$ \displaystyle(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a}F)(x,\nu) \displaystyle:=b(x,\nu,a)\cdot\nabla_{x}F(x,\nu)+\frac{1}{2}\,\Sigma(x,\nu,a):D_{xx}^{2}F(x,\nu) \displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\Bigl[b(\eta,\nu,a)\cdot\partial_{\nu}F(x,\nu)(\eta)+\frac{1}{2}\,\Sigma(\eta,\nu,a):D_{\eta}\partial_{\nu}F(x,\nu)(\eta)\Bigr]\nu(d\eta), $$

$$ \sup_{\tau\in[0,\Delta t]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[|(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a})^{2}F(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau})|\right]<\infty. $$

Then

$$ \frac{\mathbb{E}[F(s_{\Delta t},\mu_{\Delta t})]-F(s,\mu)}{\Delta t}=(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a}F)(s,\mu)+R_{F}^{a,\Delta t}(s,\mu), $$

where

$$ |R_{F}^{a,\Delta t}(s,\mu)|\leq\frac{\Delta t}{2}\sup_{\tau\in[0,\Delta t]}\mathbb{E}\!\left[|(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a})^{2}F(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau})|\right]. $$

$$ \frac{\mathbb{E}[F_{k}(s_{\Delta t},\mu_{\Delta t})]-F_{k}(s,\mu)}{\Delta t}=\hat{b}_{k}(s,\mu,a),\qquad(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a}F_{k})(s,\mu)=b_{k}(s,\mu,a), $$

$$ \hat{b}_{k}(s,\mu,a)-b_{k}(s,\mu,a)=R_{F_{k}}^{a,\Delta t}(s,\mu),\qquad\hat{\Sigma}_{ij}(s,\mu,a)-\Sigma_{ij}(s,\mu,a)=R_{G_{ij}^{s}}^{a,\Delta t}(s,\mu). $$

$$ F(s_{t},\mu_{t})=F(s,\mu)+\int_{0}^{t}(\mathscr{L}_{b,\Sigma}^{a}F)(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau})\,d\tau+M_{t}^{F}, $$

$$ M_{t}^{F}=\int_{0}^{t}\nabla_{x}F(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau})\sigma(s_{\tau},\mu_{\tau},a)\,dB_{\tau}. $$

$$ h^{\pi}(s,\mu):=\int_{\mathcal{A}}h(s,\mu,a)p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)\nu(da). $$

$$ \nabla_{s}h^{\pi}=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl[(\nabla_{s}h)p_{\pi}+h\nabla_{s}p_{\pi}\bigr]\,\nu(da), $$

$$ D_{ss}^{2}h^{\pi}=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl[(D_{ss}^{2}h)p_{\pi}+(\nabla_{s}h)\otimes(\nabla_{s}p_{\pi})+(\nabla_{s}p_{\pi})\otimes(\nabla_{s}h)+hD_{ss}^{2}p_{\pi}\bigr]\,\nu(da), $$

and

$$ \partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(\xi)=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl[\partial_{\mu}h(\xi)p_{\pi}+h\partial_{\mu}p_{\pi}(\xi)\bigr]\,\nu(da),\qquad D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(\xi)=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\bigl[D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h(\xi)p_{\pi}+hD_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}p_{\pi}(\xi)\bigr]\,\nu(da). $$

Here all terms are evaluated at $(s,\mu,a)$ , except the Lions derivatives, which are evaluated at $(s,\mu,a,\xi)$ . The uniform bounds on $h$ and its derivatives, together with the bound by $\ell_{*}$ , give

$$ \|\nabla_{s}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|+\|D_{ss}^{2}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)\|+|\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)|+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)\|\leq K_{*}. $$

$$ |AB-\bar{A}\bar{B}|\leq|A-\bar{A}|\,|B|+|\bar{A}|\,|B-\bar{B}|. $$

For instance, in the term $\int_{\mathcal{A}}(\nabla_{s}h)p_{\pi}\,\nu(da)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|(\nabla_{s}h)(s,\mu,a)p_{\pi}(a\mid s,\mu)-(\nabla_{s}h)(\bar{s},\bar{\mu},a)p_{\pi}(a\mid\bar{s},\bar{\mu})\right|\leq C_{R}d(Z,\bar{Z})\ell_{*}(a)+C\,\ell_{*,R}(a)d(Z,\bar{Z}). $$

The right-hand side is integrable with respect to $\nu(da)$ . The same argument applies to each product appearing in the four formulas above, using the local Lipschitz bounds for $h$ and its derivatives and the $L^{1}(\nu)$ local Lipschitz bounds for $p_{\pi}$ and its derivatives. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla_{s}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)-\nabla_{s}h^{\pi}(\bar{s},\bar{\mu})\|+\|D_{ss}^{2}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)-D_{ss}^{2}h^{\pi}(\bar{s},\bar{\mu})\| \displaystyle+|\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)-\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(\bar{s},\bar{\mu})(\bar{\xi})|+\|D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(s,\mu)(\xi)-D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}h^{\pi}(\bar{s},\bar{\mu})(\bar{\xi})\|\leq C_{*,R}d(Z,\bar{Z}). $$

This proves the auxiliary statement.

Applying the auxiliary statement to $h=b_{i}$ , for $i=1,\dots,d$ , gives the required boundedness and local Lipschitz regularity of $b^{\pi}$ . Applying the same statement to $h=\Sigma_{ij}$ , for $i,j=1,\dots,d$ , gives the corresponding properties for $\Sigma^{\pi}$ . $$ \nabla_{s}\sigma^{\pi}=D\Psi(\Sigma^{\pi})[\nabla_{s}\Sigma^{\pi}], $$

$$ D_{ss}^{2}\sigma^{\pi}=D\Psi(\Sigma^{\pi})[D_{ss}^{2}\Sigma^{\pi}]+D^{2}\Psi(\Sigma^{\pi})[\nabla_{s}\Sigma^{\pi},\nabla_{s}\Sigma^{\pi}], $$

$$ \partial_{\mu}\sigma^{\pi}(\xi)=D\Psi(\Sigma^{\pi})[\partial_{\mu}\Sigma^{\pi}(\xi)],\qquad D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\sigma^{\pi}(\xi)=D\Psi(\Sigma^{\pi})[D_{\xi}\partial_{\mu}\Sigma^{\pi}(\xi)]. $$

#### Proposition A.9 (Auxiliary control problem).

Let $\Delta t_{0}>0$ be given by Lemma A.8, and let $\Delta t\in(0,\Delta t_{0}]$ . Consider the auxiliary control problem

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{V}}^{\mathrm{aux}}(\mu):=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm{add}}}\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\hat{\mu}_{t})\,dt\,\bigg|\,\hat{\mu}_{0}=\mu\right],\qquad\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), $$

where $r_{\lambda}^{\pi}$ is defined in (3), with $r$ as in (23), and $(\hat{\mu}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ is generated by

$$ d\hat{s}_{t}=\hat{b}^{\pi}(\hat{s}_{t},\hat{\mu}_{t})\,dt,\qquad\hat{s}_{0}\sim\mu,\qquad\hat{\mu}_{t}=\Law(\hat{s}_{t}), $$

with

$$ \hat{b}^{\pi}(s,\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}\hat{b}(s,\mu,a)\,\pi(da\mid s,\mu), $$

and $\hat{b}$ defined in (32). Then the auxiliary control problem admits an optimal Gaussian feedback policy

$$ \hat{\pi}^{*}(\cdot\mid s,\mu)=\mathcal{N}\left(-N^{-1}\hat{B}^{\top}\bigl(\hat{K}(s-\bar{\mu})+\hat{\Lambda}\bar{\mu}\bigr),\frac{\lambda}{2}N^{-1}\right), $$

where $\hat{K}$ and $\hat{\Lambda}$ are the stabilizing solutions of (84) and (85), respectively. Moreover, $\widehat{\mathcal{V}}^{\mathrm{aux}}(\mu)=\hat{\mathcal{V}}^{*}(\mu)$ for every $\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Consequently, (89) is an optimal LQR-MF-PhiBE policy.

#### Proof.

By Lemma A.8, for every $\Delta t\in(0,\Delta t_{0}]$ , Assumption 5.2 holds with $(A,\bar{A},B)$ replaced by $(\hat{A},\hat{\bar{A}},\hat{B})$ . Hence Proposition 5.4, applied to this auxiliary LQR problem, yields the Gaussian feedback (89) and the optimal value $\widehat{\mathcal{V}}^{\mathrm{aux}}$ .

It remains to identify the auxiliary performance with the LQR-MF-PhiBE evaluation. Let $\pi$ belong to the policy class specified in Definition 5.7, and write

$$ \widehat{\mathcal{J}}^{\pi}(\mu):=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\hat{\mu}_{t})\,dt\,\bigg|\,\hat{\mu}_{0}=\mu\right]. $$

The auxiliary law flow has generator $\mathcal{L}_{\hat{b},0}^{\pi}$ , so $\widehat{\mathcal{J}}^{\pi}$ solves

$$ (\mathcal{L}_{\hat{b},0}^{\pi}-\beta)\widehat{\mathcal{J}}^{\pi}+r_{\lambda}^{\pi}=0. $$

$$ U(\mu)=e^{-\beta T}U(\hat{\mu}_{T})+\int_{0}^{T}e^{-\beta t}r_{\lambda}^{\pi}(\hat{\mu}_{t})\,dt. $$

Polynomial growth and the auxiliary transversality condition imply that the boundary term converges to zero. Hence $U=\widehat{\mathcal{J}}^{\pi}$ , and therefore

$$ \hat{\mathcal{V}}^{\pi}=\widehat{\mathcal{J}}^{\pi}. $$

Taking the supremum over the common policy class in Definition 5.7 gives

$$ \hat{\mathcal{V}}^{*}=\widehat{\mathcal{V}}^{\mathrm{aux}}. $$

Since (89) attains the auxiliary supremum, it is an optimal LQR-MF-PhiBE policy. ∎

The following lemma gives explicit bounds on the perturbation constants associated with the discounted CARE. These bounds will be used below to display the dependence on $\beta$ .

#### Lemma A.10 (Explicit bounds for the ARE perturbation constants).

Let $Q_{0}\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}$ , $G\in\mathbb{S}_{+}^{d}$ , and $A_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ . Let $\beta\geq 0$ , set $A_{\beta}:=A_{0}-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d}$ , and let $X\in\mathbb{S}_{++}^{d}$ be the stabilizing solution of

$$ Q_{0}+A_{\beta}^{\top}X+XA_{\beta}-XGX=0. $$

Define $\Phi_{X}:=A_{\beta}-GX,$ and $\mathcal{L}_{X}W:=\Phi_{X}^{\top}W+W\Phi_{X}.$ Let $l_{X},p_{X},q_{X}$ be the corresponding perturbation constants in the sense of [53, Theorem 3.1], namely

$$ l_{X}:=\|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}\|^{-1},\qquad p_{X}:=\left\|Z\mapsto\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}(XZ+Z^{\top}X)\right\|,\qquad q_{X}:=\left\|H\mapsto\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}(XHX)\right\|. $$

Then

$$ l_{X}\geq\frac{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}{\|X\|^{2}},\qquad p_{X}\leq\frac{2\|X\|^{3}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})},\qquad q_{X}\leq\frac{\|X\|^{4}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}. $$

Moreover,

$$ \frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}(X)}\leq\frac{\beta+2\|A_{0}\|+\|G\|\|X\|}{\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}. $$

Consequently,

$$ l_{X}\geq\frac{\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})^{2}}{\|X\|^{2}\bigl(\beta+2\|A_{0}\|+\|G\|\|X\|\bigr)}, $$

and

$$ p_{X}\leq\frac{2\|X\|^{3}\bigl(\beta+2\|A_{0}\|+\|G\|\|X\|\bigr)}{\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})^{2}}, $$

$$ q_{X}\leq\frac{\|X\|^{4}\bigl(\beta+2\|A_{0}\|+\|G\|\|X\|\bigr)}{\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})^{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $X$ solves (90), we have

$$ A_{\beta}^{\top}X+XA_{\beta}-XGX=-Q_{0}. $$

Therefore, with $\Phi_{X}=A_{\beta}-GX$ ,

$$ \Phi_{X}^{\top}X+X\Phi_{X}=-Q_{0}-XGX\preceq-Q_{0}. $$

Let $z(t):=e^{\Phi_{X}t}z_{0}$ . From (96),

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\,z(t)^{\top}Xz(t)=z(t)^{\top}\bigl(\Phi_{X}^{\top}X+X\Phi_{X}\bigr)z(t)\leq-\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})\|z(t)\|^{2}. $$

Since $z^{\top}Xz\leq\|X\|\|z\|^{2}$ , it follows that

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\,z(t)^{\top}Xz(t)\leq-\frac{\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}{\|X\|}z(t)^{\top}Xz(t). $$

Thus

$$ z(t)^{\top}Xz(t)\leq e^{-\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})t/\|X\|}z_{0}^{\top}Xz_{0}. $$

Using $z(t)^{\top}Xz(t)\geq\lambda_{\min}(X)\|z(t)\|^{2}$ and $z_{0}^{\top}Xz_{0}\leq\|X\|\|z_{0}\|^{2}$ , we obtain

$$ \|e^{\Phi_{X}t}\|^{2}\leq\frac{\|X\|}{\lambda_{\min}(X)}e^{-\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})t/\|X\|},\qquad t\geq 0. $$

For every symmetric matrix $Y$ , the solution of $\mathcal{L}_{X}W=Y$ is

$$ W=-\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\Phi_{X}^{\top}t}Ye^{\Phi_{X}t}\,dt. $$

Therefore, by (97),

$$ \|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}Y\|\leq\int_{0}^{\infty}\|e^{\Phi_{X}t}\|^{2}\,dt\,\|Y\|\leq\frac{\|X\|^{2}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}\|Y\|. $$

Hence

$$ \|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}\|\leq\frac{\|X\|^{2}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}, $$

which gives the first term in (91).

Next, for any $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ ,

$$ \|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}(XZ+Z^{\top}X)\|\leq\|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}\|\bigl(\|XZ\|+\|Z^{\top}X\|\bigr)\leq\frac{2\|X\|^{3}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}\|Z\|. $$

This proves the estimate for $p_{X}$ . Similarly, for any $H\in\mathbb{S}^{d}$ ,

$$ \|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}(XHX)\|\leq\|\mathcal{L}_{X}^{-1}\|\,\|X\|^{2}\,\|H\|\leq\frac{\|X\|^{4}}{\lambda_{\min}(X)\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})}\|H\|. $$

This proves the estimate for $q_{X}$ .

It remains to prove (92). Let $v$ be a unit eigenvector of $X$ associated with $\lambda_{\min}(X)$ . Evaluating (90) on $v$ gives

$$ 0=v^{\top}Q_{0}v+2v^{\top}XA_{\beta}v-v^{\top}XGXv. $$

Since $Xv=\lambda_{\min}(X)v$ and $A_{\beta}=A_{0}-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d}$ , we get

$$ 0=v^{\top}Q_{0}v+2\lambda_{\min}(X)v^{\top}A_{0}v-\beta\lambda_{\min}(X)-\lambda_{\min}(X)^{2}v^{\top}Gv. $$

Hence

$$ v^{\top}Q_{0}v=\beta\lambda_{\min}(X)+\lambda_{\min}(X)^{2}v^{\top}Gv-2\lambda_{\min}(X)v^{\top}A_{0}v. $$

Using $v^{\top}Q_{0}v\geq\lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})$ , $v^{\top}Gv\leq\|G\|$ , and $-v^{\top}A_{0}v\leq\|A_{0}\|$ , we obtain

$$ \lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})\leq\bigl(\beta+2\|A_{0}\|\bigr)\lambda_{\min}(X)+\|G\|\lambda_{\min}(X)^{2}. $$

Since $\lambda_{\min}(X)\leq\|X\|$ , this implies

$$ \lambda_{\min}(Q_{0})\leq\bigl(\beta+2\|A_{0}\|+\|G\|\|X\|\bigr)\lambda_{\min}(X), $$

which proves (92). Finally, (93) follows by combining the first term in (91) with (92), and (94)-(95) follow by combining (91) with (92). ∎

Let $L:=N^{-1}B^{\top}K$ , $\hat{L}:=N^{-1}\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{K}$ , $U:=N^{-1}B^{\top}\Lambda$ , and $\hat{U}:=N^{-1}\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{\Lambda}$ . By (112), the feedback means of $\pi^{*}$ and $\hat{\pi}^{*}$ are

$$ \displaystyle m^{*}(x,\nu)=-L(x-\bar{\nu})-U\bar{\nu},\qquad\hat{m}^{*}(x,\nu)=-\hat{L}(x-\bar{\nu})-\hat{U}\bar{\nu}. $$

The two Gaussian policies have covariance $\frac{\lambda}{2}N^{-1}$ . Hence, using (23) and (3), there exists a constant $c_{\lambda,N}$ , independent of $\nu$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle r_{\lambda}^{\pi^{*}}(\nu)=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((Q+L^{\top}NL)\operatorname{Cov}(\nu)\bigr)-\bar{\nu}^{\top}(Q+\bar{Q}+U^{\top}NU)\bar{\nu}+c_{\lambda,N}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle r_{\lambda}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\nu)=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((Q+\hat{L}^{\top}N\hat{L})\operatorname{Cov}(\nu)\bigr)-\bar{\nu}^{\top}(Q+\bar{Q}+\hat{U}^{\top}N\hat{U})\bar{\nu}+c_{\lambda,N}. $$

Let $(\hat{\mu}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be the law flow generated by the original dynamics under $\hat{\pi}^{*}$ , and set $\hat{C}_{t}:=\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\mu}_{t})$ . From (114), the mean and covariance satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\bar{\hat{\mu}}}_{t}=(A+\bar{A}-B\hat{U})\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t},\qquad\dot{\hat{C}}_{t}=(A-B\hat{L})\hat{C}_{t}+\hat{C}_{t}(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}+\gamma\gamma^{\top}. $$

Moreover, by the explicit LQR value formula,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\nu)=-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(K\operatorname{Cov}(\nu)\bigr)-\bar{\nu}^{\top}\Lambda\bar{\nu}-R. $$

Using (118) along the flow $(\hat{\mu}_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ and integrating by parts, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\mu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left[-\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})+\beta\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})\right]dt. $$

Therefore, by the definition of $\mathcal{V}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\mu)-\mathcal{V}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\mu)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left[-\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})+\beta\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})-r_{\lambda}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})\right]dt. $$

We compute the integrand in (120). Using (117), (116), and (118), we get

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})+\beta\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})-r_{\lambda}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\hat{\mu}_{t})=\operatorname{Tr}\Bigl(\bigl[(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}K+K(A-B\hat{L})-\beta K+Q+\hat{L}^{\top}N\hat{L}\bigr]\hat{C}_{t}\Bigr) \displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}^{\top}\bigl[(A+\bar{A}-B\hat{U})^{\top}\Lambda+\Lambda(A+\bar{A}-B\hat{U})-\beta\Lambda+Q+\bar{Q}+\hat{U}^{\top}N\hat{U}\bigr]\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad-\beta R+\gamma^{\top}K\gamma-c_{\lambda,N}. $$

The scalar term in (121) vanishes by (27). We next simplify the two matrix residuals in (121). Since (25) is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle(A-BL)^{\top}K+K(A-BL)-\beta K+Q+L^{\top}NL=0, $$

inserting $K$ into the closed-loop equation associated with $\hat{L}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}K+K(A-B\hat{L})-\beta K+Q \displaystyle+\hat{L}^{\top}N\hat{L}=(A-BL)^{\top}K+K(A-BL)-\beta K+Q+L^{\top}NL \displaystyle-(\hat{L}-L)^{\top}B^{\top}K-KB(\hat{L}-L)+\hat{L}^{\top}N\hat{L}-L^{\top}NL. $$

The first line on the right-hand side of (123) vanishes by (122). Since $L=N^{-1}B^{\top}K$ , we have $B^{\top}K=NL$ and $KB=L^{\top}N$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}K+K(A-B\hat{L})-\beta K+Q+\hat{L}^{\top}N\hat{L}=(\hat{L}-L)^{\top}N(\hat{L}-L). $$

Similarly, (26) is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle(A+\bar{A}-BU)^{\top}\Lambda+\Lambda(A+\bar{A}-BU)-\beta\Lambda+Q+\bar{Q}+U^{\top}NU=0. $$

Inserting $\Lambda$ into the closed-loop equation associated with $\hat{U}$ and using $U=N^{-1}B^{\top}\Lambda$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle(A+\bar{A}-B\hat{U})^{\top}\Lambda+\Lambda(A+\bar{A}-B\hat{U})-\beta\Lambda+Q+\bar{Q}+\hat{U}^{\top}N\hat{U}=(\hat{U}-U)^{\top}N(\hat{U}-U). $$

Substituting (124) and (126) into (121), and then into (120), yields

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\mu)-\mathcal{V}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\mu) \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((\hat{L}-L)^{\top}N(\hat{L}-L)\hat{C}_{t}\bigr)dt+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}^{\top}(\hat{U}-U)^{\top}N(\hat{U}-U)\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}\,dt. $$

In particular, $\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\mu)-\mathcal{V}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\mu)\geq 0.$ It remains to estimate the right-hand side of (127). From Step 4, we have already proved

$$ \displaystyle\|B^{\top}K-\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{K}\|\leq C\Delta t,\qquad\|B^{\top}\Lambda-\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{\Lambda}\|\leq C\Delta t. $$

Therefore, by the definitions of $L,\hat{L},U,\hat{U}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{L}-L\|+\|\hat{U}-U\| \displaystyle\leq\|N^{-1}\|\left(\|\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{K}-B^{\top}K\|+\|\hat{B}^{\top}\hat{\Lambda}-B^{\top}\Lambda\|\right)\leq C\Delta t. $$

Because $K$ and $\Lambda$ are the stabilizing solutions of the discounted CAREs, the shifted matrices

$$ A_{\beta}-BL,\qquad\widetilde{A}_{\beta}-BU,\qquad A_{\beta}:=A-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d},\quad\widetilde{A}_{\beta}:=A+\bar{A}-\frac{\beta}{2}I_{d}, $$

are Hurwitz. Since $\hat{L}\to L$ and $\hat{U}\to U$ , after decreasing $\Delta t_{*}$ there exist $C,c>0$ , independent of $\Delta t$ , such that

$$ \|e^{(A_{\beta}-B\hat{L})t}\|+\|e^{(\widetilde{A}_{\beta}-B\hat{U})t}\|\leq Ce^{-ct},\qquad t\geq 0. $$

The mean equation in (117) therefore gives

$$ e^{-\beta t}|\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}|^{2}=\left|e^{(\widetilde{A}_{\beta}-B\hat{U})t}\bar{\mu}\right|^{2}\leq Ce^{-2ct}|\bar{\mu}|^{2}. $$

For the covariance, variation of constants yields

$$ \hat{C}_{t}=e^{(A-B\hat{L})t}\operatorname{Cov}(\mu)e^{(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}t}+\int_{0}^{t}e^{(A-B\hat{L})u}\gamma\gamma^{\top}e^{(A-B\hat{L})^{\top}u}\,du. $$

Consequently,

$$ e^{-\beta t}\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{C}_{t})\leq Ce^{-2ct}\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(\mu))+C|\gamma|^{2}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\beta(t-u)}e^{-2cu}\,du. $$

Since $\beta>0$ , integration in time and Fubini’s theorem give

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left(\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{C}_{t})+|\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}|^{2}\right)dt\leq C\bigl(1+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr), $$

with $C$ independent of $\Delta t$ . The same pointwise estimates imply

$$ e^{-\beta t}\left(\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{C}_{t})+|\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}|^{2}\right)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad t\to\infty, $$

and hence justify the boundary limit used in (119). Combining (127), (129), and (130), we get

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\mathcal{V}^{\pi^{*}}(\mu)-\mathcal{V}^{\hat{\pi}^{*}}(\mu) \displaystyle\leq C\left(\|\hat{L}-L\|^{2}+\|\hat{U}-U\|^{2}\right)\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\beta t}\left(\operatorname{Tr}(\hat{C}_{t})+|\bar{\hat{\mu}}_{t}|^{2}\right)dt\leq C\Delta t^{2}\bigl(1+m_{2}(\mu)\bigr). $$

This proves (36). ∎

#### Lemma A.11 (Second-moment bound for the MKV-LQR flow when $\beta=0$ ).

Assume Assumption 5.2 with $\beta=0$ . Let $(K,\Lambda)$ be the stabilizing solution of (25)-(26), and let $\pi^{*}$ be the Gaussian feedback in (29). Let $(s_{t},\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}$ be the MKV dynamics (5) under $\pi^{*}$ , with $\Law(s_{t})=\mu_{t}$ and $\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})$ . Then there exist constants $C\geq 1$ and $\kappa>0$ such that, for every $t\geq 0$ ,

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{t})\leq Ce^{-2\kappa t}m_{2}(\mu_{0})+C|\gamma|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $\bar{\mu}_{t}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}x\,\mu_{t}(dx)$ and set $\xi_{t}:=s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t}$ . Under (29), $\int_{\mathbb{R}^{m}}a\pi^{*}(da\mid x,\mu)=-N^{-1}B^{\top}\bigl(K(x-\bar{\mu})+\Lambda\bar{\mu}\bigr).$ Since $\sigma(x,\mu,a)=\gamma$ , the closed-loop MKV dynamics is

$$ ds_{t}=\bigl[A_{K}(s_{t}-\bar{\mu}_{t})+A_{\Lambda}\bar{\mu}_{t}\bigr]dt+\gamma\,dW_{t}, $$

where $A_{K}:=A-BN^{-1}B^{\top}K$ and $A_{\Lambda}:=A+\bar{A}-BN^{-1}B^{\top}\Lambda.$ Taking expectation gives $\dot{\bar{\mu}}_{t}=A_{\Lambda}\bar{\mu}_{t}$ . Since $\Lambda$ is the stabilizing solution of (26), $A_{\Lambda}$ is Hurwitz. Hence there exist $C_{\Lambda}\geq 1$ and $\kappa_{\Lambda}>0$ such that

$$ |\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}\leq C_{\Lambda}e^{-2\kappa_{\Lambda}t}|\bar{\mu}_{0}|^{2}. $$

The estimate for $\xi_{t}$ follows from the same quadratic energy argument used in [12, Lemma A.8]. Indeed, $\xi_{t}$ solves

$$ d\xi_{t}=A_{K}\xi_{t}\,dt+\gamma\,dW_{t}, $$

and the stabilizing property of $K$ gives a Lyapunov function for $A_{K}$ . Applying Itô’s formula to this quadratic Lyapunov function and using Gronwall’s inequality yields constants $C_{K}\geq 1$ and $\kappa_{K}>0$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}|\xi_{t}|^{2}\leq C_{K}e^{-2\kappa_{K}t}\mathbb{E}|\xi_{0}|^{2}+C_{K}|\gamma|^{2}. $$

Finally, since $m_{2}(\mu_{t})=\mathbb{E}|s_{t}|^{2}=\mathbb{E}|\xi_{t}|^{2}+|\bar{\mu}_{t}|^{2}$ and $m_{2}(\mu_{0})=\mathbb{E}|\xi_{0}|^{2}+|\bar{\mu}_{0}|^{2},$ taking $\kappa:=\min\{\kappa_{K},\kappa_{\Lambda}\}$ and increasing $C$ if necessary gives

$$ m_{2}(\mu_{t})\leq Ce^{-2\kappa t}m_{2}(\mu_{0})+C|\gamma|^{2}. $$
